# Quick Transition

```{r}
#We move on to R's basic "data objects": how values are stored, how R silently mixes types together (coercion), and how we represent variables as "factors" in R.
```

# Atomic Vectors

```{r}
#An "atomic vector" is a one-dimensional sequence of values of the same type. 
#We build one with c() -- remember our "die" object? That was actually an atomic vector too.
#“c() stands for combine — it combines (glues together) separate values into a single vector.”

die <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
die

is.vector(die)  ## TRUE
length(die)     ## 6
```

```{r}
#Even a single value is really just a vector of length 1:

five <- 5
is.vector(five) ## TRUE
length(five)    ## 1
```

```{r}
#names() lets you attach labels to a vector's elements. 
##This does NOT change the values, it just adds a label on top of them.

names(die) <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six")
die

die + 1  #Names survive operations too
## "one" still labels the 1st slot -- but its value is now 2, not 1. Labels stick to positions, not to specific numbers.

names(die) <- NULL  #Assign NULL to remove the names
die
```

```{r}
#Why label at all? 
##So you can refer to an element by a meaningful name instead of remembering its position number -- e.g. die["three"] instead of die[3]. 
##This becomes especially useful later with survey items, regression coefficients, or table() output, where names are added automatically.
```


```{r}
ages <- c(23, 19, 31, 27)
names(ages) <- c("Aylin", "Baran", "Cem", "Deniz")
ages

#Without names, you'd have to remember "Cem is the 3rd participant":
ages[3]        ## 31 -- but which participant is this? You'd have to check.

#With names, it's self-explanatory:
ages["Cem"]    ## 31 -- immediately clear whose age this is

#Names also stay correctly attached during operations -- e.g. everyone's age next year:
ages + 1       ## Aylin=24, Baran=20, Cem=32, Deniz=28 -- still the right label on the right person
```



# Types of Vectors

```{r}
#Before we look at coercion, let's quickly meet the four basic types a vector can hold.

colors <- c("red", "blue", "green")   #CHARACTER -- text, always shown in quotes
colors
typeof(colors)  ## "character"

scores <- c(88.5, 92, 76.3)           #NUMERIC (technically "double") -- numbers, decimals allowed, no quotes
scores
typeof(scores)  ## "double"

passed <- c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE)        #LOGICAL -- only TRUE/FALSE, no quotes
passed
typeof(passed)  ## "logical"
```


```{r}
#INTEGER is a special case of numeric: whole numbers only, no decimals. 
#R usually gives you "double" by default -- you get "integer" mainly when you use : to build a sequence (like our die!), or add an L after a number.

die <- 1:6
typeof(die)   ## "integer" -- because we used ":"

typeof(5)     ## "double"  -- a plain number is double by default
typeof(5L)    ## "integer" -- the L forces it to be integer

#So "numeric" is really an umbrella term covering both double and integer.
```

```{r}
#A quick note on terminology, since it differs from SPSS:
#SPSS's nominal/ordinal/scale describe what a variable MEANS (measurement level).
#R's character/double/integer/logical describe how a value is STORED (data type) -- a separate question.
#Integer just means "whole number, stored efficiently" -- it says nothing about whether the variable is nominal, ordinal, or continuous.
#Rough mapping: SPSS "scale" variables usually become double in R; SPSS nominal/ordinal categories are usually represented as factors (which, as we just saw, store integers underneath).
```

```{r}
#A quick note on terminology, since it differs from jamovi:
#jamovi's Nominal/Ordinal/Continuous describe what a variable MEANS (measurement level).
#R's character/double/integer/logical describe how a value is STORED (data type) -- a separate question.
#Integer just means "whole number, stored efficiently" -- it says nothing about whether the variable is nominal, ordinal, or continuous.
#Rough mapping: jamovi "Continuous" variables usually become double in R; jamovi Nominal/Ordinal categories are usually represented as factors (which, as we just saw, store integers underneath).
```


```{r}
#Now that we know these four types, watch what happens when we put more than one type into the SAME vector:
```

# Coercion

```{r}
#In R, ALL elements of an atomic vector must be the same type. 
##If you mix types, R silently converts everything to the "most flexible" type: character > numeric > logical.

card <- c("ace", "hearts", 1)
card  ## Everything became "character" -- even the 1 turned into the string "1"
```

```{r}
#Logical values turn into 1/0 when mixed with numbers. That's why summing a logical vector counts the TRUEs:

sum(c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))  ## 2
```

```{r}
#Instead of relying on silent coercion, you can also convert explicitly:

as.character(1)    ## "1"
as.logical(1)      ## TRUE
as.numeric(FALSE)  ## 0

```

# Factors -- Translating Psychological Variables into Code

```{r}
#We represent categorical psychological variables (experimental condition, education level, etc.) as "factors" in R. 
#Under the hood, a factor is really an integer vector -- with a "levels" attribute acting as a label on top.

condition <- factor(c("treatment", "control", "control", "treatment"))
condition

typeof(condition)   ## "integer" -- surprising, right? It looks like text but it's actually numbers.
attributes(condition)

#A factor is really just an integer vector wearing a costume: typeof() shows the raw integers underneath, while class() = "factor" tells R to display each integer using its levels label instead of the number itself.
```

```{r}
#unclass() shows you what a factor REALLY stores underneath:

unclass(condition)
```

```{r}
#WATCH OUT -- a common student mistake: as.character() converts a factor to its DISPLAYED label, not to the underlying integer code:

as.character(condition)  ## "treatment" "control" "control" "treatment"

condition_chr <- as.character(condition)
typeof(condition_chr)
```
